title: Sampling and retention
summary: Agent traces are large, so most systems keep only a share. Head sampling decides at the start of a trace, tail sampling decides after seeing it, and metrics are never sampled. Retention tiers then set how long what you kept stays searchable.
useIf: Trace volume or cost is climbing and you must decide what to keep, for how long and where totals will come from.
avoidIf: You compute token totals from sampled traces or sample so hard that the failing runs vanish.

explain.md: **Head sampling** decides as early as possible, without looking at the whole trace. The common form is consistent probability sampling by trace id, for example 5 percent, which keeps or drops whole traces. It is simple and cheap, but it cannot guarantee that traces containing errors are kept. **Tail sampling** decides after all or most spans of a trace are complete, so it can always keep errors, keep slow traces and apply different rates per service. It needs a stateful collector component, is harder to operate and tends to be vendor specific. Large systems often combine them: a coarse head sample protects the pipeline and tail sampling makes the fine decisions [[r20]].

In Application Insights the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro for .NET, Node.js and Python defaults to **rate-limited sampling at five traces per second** for Azure Monitor export. You can choose a fixed ratio between 0 and 1 or a rate limit. Python reads `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` and `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG`, not the older `sampling_ratio` and `traces_per_second`. If unsure, start with a fixed 5 percent (0.05). **Metrics are not sampled**, so alert on metrics. Ingestion sampling and a daily cap are last-resort cost guards. An App Service tutorial says the exporter applies adaptive sampling by default, but the sampling page is the more authoritative source [[r15]].

explain.title: Check how much telemetry survives sampling (Microsoft Learn query)
explain.code:
union requests,dependencies,pageViews,browserTimings,exceptions,traces
| where timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize RetainedPercentage = 100/avg(itemCount) by bin(timestamp, 1h), itemType
explain.caption: Weight sums by `itemCount` when you total token attributes from retained spans.

explain.md: Retention is a separate dial. The Foundry portal Traces tab shows 90 days, while backend retention follows your Application Insights settings [[r12]]. Keep long retention for metrics and aggregated views, short retention for detailed traces, and the shortest for any stored content (see content capture, redaction and privacy).

use: Head sampling at a fixed ratio when volume is high and failures are not rare
Tail sampling in a collector when you must keep all errors and slow runs
Unsampled metrics for totals, SLIs and alerts, plus sampled traces for explanation
avoid: Do not sample at all if you produce tens of small traces per second or are legally barred from dropping data
Do not total tokens or cost from sampled spans without weighting by `itemCount`
Do not use ingestion sampling or a daily cap as your main strategy
flips: Failures are rare and you must keep every one: switch from head to tail sampling
A load test looks incomplete: raise the rate limit or use a fixed ratio for the test, since bursts above five traces per second are dropped by default
Volume is small: keep everything and skip the operational cost of a sampler

pitfalls.symptom: A load test shows far fewer traces than requests
pitfalls.cause: Rate-limited sampling at five traces per second drops bursts above that rate
pitfalls.fix: Use a fixed ratio or a higher rate limit for the test and confirm with the retained-percentage query [[r15]]

pitfalls.symptom: The traces you wanted, the errors, are missing
pitfalls.cause: Head sampling decided before the error happened
pitfalls.fix: Add tail sampling that keeps error and slow traces [[r20]]

pitfalls.symptom: Token totals computed from spans are far too low
pitfalls.cause: The sums ignore that spans are sampled
pitfalls.fix: Use unsampled counters for totals, or weight span sums by `itemCount` [[r15]]

scenarios.title: Two thousand traces per second and rare failures
scenarios.situation: An agent platform emits about 2,000 traces per second. Failures are well under 1 percent but each one matters. Storage cost is the main complaint.
unknowns: Can the team run a collector?
Does the backend offer tail sampling?
scenarios.question: What sampling do you use?

options.name: Tail sampling that keeps all errors and slow runs plus a small baseline share, with unsampled metrics for totals
options.why: It keeps the traces that matter and cuts cost on the healthy majority.
options.tradeoff: A stateful collector tier to run, monitor and scale.

options.name: Fixed 5 percent head sampling
options.why: Cheap, simple and keeps whole traces.
options.tradeoff: Drops about 95 percent of failures along with healthy traces.

options.name: Keep everything and set a daily ingestion cap
options.why: The cap drops data by time of day, not by value, and cost stays high until it triggers.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable as an emergency guard on top of a real strategy.

flips.if: No team can operate a collector
flips.then: Use head sampling and alert on error metrics.

flips.if: Volume falls below tens of traces per second

scenarios.takeaway: Keep by value when failures are rare.

scenarios.title: A regulated workflow that may not drop traces
scenarios.situation: An internal approval workflow produces 30 small traces per second. Auditors require every run to be reconstructable for a year, but content must not be stored in traces.
unknowns: Can unsampled data go to cheap storage?
What detail must a reconstruction contain?
scenarios.question: How do you handle volume and retention?

options.name: No sampling, shape-only spans, tiered retention (short hot, long cold storage)
options.why: At this volume sampling saves little and the audit needs every run.
options.tradeoff: Higher storage cost and a tiering design.

options.name: 5 percent head sampling
options.why: It drops 95 percent of runs, which violates the audit requirement.
options.tradeoff: Right for volumes where dropping is allowed.

options.name: Tail sampling that keeps errors only

flips.if: Volume grows to thousands per second
flips.then: Route unsampled data to low-cost storage and keep sampled data hot.

scenarios.takeaway: When you may not drop data, spend on retention tiers instead of sampling.

scenarios.title: A load test with missing traces
scenarios.situation: A load test sends 100 requests per second for ten minutes. The backend shows far fewer traces than requests, and the team suspects data loss in the app.
unknowns: What sampler and rate is configured?
scenarios.question: What do you check and change?

options.name: Check the sampler settings and retained percentage, then use a fixed ratio or higher rate for the test
options.why: The default rate-limited sampler caps at five traces per second, which explains the gap.
options.tradeoff: Higher volume and cost during the test.

options.name: Increase application replicas
options.why: The limit is the sampler, not capacity.
options.tradeoff: Right if requests themselves are failing.

options.name: Trust the traces and report data loss
options.why: Missing sampled traces are expected, and the app is not dropping data.
options.tradeoff: Use metrics to confirm request counts.

flips.then: The app or network is dropping load, so investigate that.
Choose the ratio deliberately and document it.

scenarios.takeaway: Know your sampler before you trust a trace count.

quiz.q: Which sampling approach can guarantee that every trace containing an error is kept?
options: Tail sampling that inspects the completed trace
quiz.explain: Head sampling decides before the trace content is known, so it cannot ensure errors are kept. Tail sampling decides after the trace completes and can keep errors and slow runs. A daily cap drops data without regard to value.

quiz.q: A sampled span stream shows RetainedPercentage of 10 percent. A retained span reports 1,000 input tokens. Roughly how many tokens does that span represent when weighted by `itemCount`?
quiz.explain: A 10 percent retention means itemCount is about 10, so each retained span stands for about 10 spans: 1,000 x 10 = 10,000 tokens.

quiz.q: Which statements about sampling in Application Insights are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro defaults to rate-limited sampling at five traces per second
Metrics are not sampled, so alerts should use metrics
Traces are never sampled by default
quiz.explain: The distro defaults to five traces per second, metrics are not sampled and Python uses the standard OTel environment variables. The fourth statement contradicts the default.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between head and tail sampling?
flashcards.back: Head decides at the start of a trace and cannot see errors. Tail decides after the trace completes, so it can keep errors and slow runs, but needs a stateful collector.

flashcards.front: What does the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro sample by default?
flashcards.back: Rate-limited sampling at five traces per second for Azure Monitor export. Bursts above that are dropped.

flashcards.front: Why alert on metrics instead of traces?
flashcards.back: Metrics are not sampled, so counts and rates are accurate. Use traces to explain an alert.
